Semiconductor

 Home Physics
OurBigBook.com Words: 9k Articles: 136
A semiconductor has an electronic band gap and a conductivity strongly affected by temperature, impurities and carrier injection. Optical absorption can create mobile electrons and holes, enabling a photodiode.
The useful feature of a semiconductor is that its charge carrier population can be controlled. Semiconductor doping changes the supply of mobile electrons or electron holes; carrier injection changes their population away from thermal equilibrium. A transistor turns that control into an electronic amplifier: a small input signal controls a larger flow of supplied energy.
For a uniform semiconductor in a weak electric field, a simple drift model writes its electrical conductivity as
σ=q(nμn​+pμp​).
(1)
Here q>0 is the elementary charge, n,p are the number densities of mobile electrons and electron holes, and μn​,μp​ their positive charge carrier mobilities. The two contributions add because opposite electric charges drift in opposite directions and therefore carry electric current in the same direction. This model assumes fixed temperature and mobilities and omits diffusion from density gradients.
An original dimensionless example isolates the effect of carrier injection. Suppose initially p≪n=n0​ and μn​=2μp​. Adding equal excess populations Δn=Δp=0.1n0​ gives Δσ/σ0​=0.15, even though the added electron holes remain a minority carrier population. A semiconductor can respond strongly to a small injected population without changing its underlying band gap.

III-V semiconductor

Words: 118 Articles: 1
Semiconductor OurBigBook.com
A compound semiconductor built from group-III and group-V elements, such as gallium arsenide. Many common members have a zinc blende structure, while other materials or growth conditions give a wurtzite structure. The chemical family alone does not fix a direct rather than indirect gap or a particular band ordering.

Zone-centre bands of a zinc-blende III-V semiconductor

Words: 73
III-V semiconductor OurBigBook.com
A common unstrained cubic III-V band ordering consists of an s-like Γ6c​ conduction doublet, a p-like Γ8v​ quartet and a lower spin-orbit split-off Γ7v​ doublet. In the cubic limit the quartet gives heavy-hole and light-hole bands that meet at the Gamma point; different curvatures and direction-dependent mixing distinguish them away from it. The split-off valence band is separated by Δso​. This common ordering is a model to check against the actual material, not a consequence of chemical stoichiometry alone.

Organic semiconductor

Words: 133 Articles: 3
Semiconductor OurBigBook.com
An organic solid supporting electronic charge transport; conjugation, intermolecular packing and disorder influence its properties.

Optical absorption in organic semiconductors

Words: 67
Organic semiconductor OurBigBook.com
Molecular excitations in organic semiconductors often retain strong local character. Weak screening supports Frenkel excitons or intermolecular charge-transfer admixtures, so a photon can create a bound neutral excitation rather than free carriers. Transition dipoles, spin selection rules, molecular packing and Franck-Condon factors set the bright spectral features. Disorder and thermal vibrations broaden them. Electronic overlap can also produce more delocalized excitons; the molecular limit is a useful model, not a definition covering every organic solid.

PCBM

Words: 27
Organic semiconductor OurBigBook.com
A soluble fullerene derivative, commonly the C60-based phenyl-C61-butyric acid methyl ester, used as an electron acceptor in organic photovoltaic blends. Different fullerene cage sizes give related derivatives.

Poly(3-hexylthiophene)

Words: 24
Organic semiconductor OurBigBook.com
A conjugated polymer with hexyl-substituted thiophene repeat units, often used as a model electron-donor semiconductor. Regioregularity and packing influence its optical and transport response.

Surface recombination

Semiconductor OurBigBook.com
Recombination of charge carriers through surface or interface states. Surface passivation and suitable wider-band-gap window or field layers can reduce minority-carrier losses in a photovoltaic device.

Surface passivation

Words: 24
Semiconductor OurBigBook.com
Reduction of electronically active surface states or of minority-carrier access to them. Chemical bond termination and electrostatic field effects can both suppress surface recombination.

Semiconductor OurBigBook.com
A contact with approximately linear, nonrectifying current–voltage behavior and suitably low contact resistance in its operating range.

Transmission line contact measurement

Ohmic contact OurBigBook.com
A pad-spacing method separating contact and sheet resistance. For uniform ohmic contacts, R(d)=2Rc​+R□​d/W; the transfer length is LT​=ρc​/R□​​. A rectifying Schottky junction requires bias-dependent analysis.

Specific contact resistivity (ρc​)

Ohmic contact OurBigBook.com
An area-normalized interface resistance, ρc​ in resistance times area. For nonlinear contacts specify the bias-dependent differential quantity.

Schottky barrier

Semiconductor OurBigBook.com
An energy barrier at a metal–semiconductor contact. Depletion width and tunneling depend on doping; interface states can limit simple work-function predictions.

Nondegenerate semiconductor

Words: 31
Semiconductor OurBigBook.com
A carrier regime in which conduction electrons and valence holes are dilute enough to use Boltzmann approximations to Fermi-Dirac occupations. Typically Ec​−μ≫kB​T and μ−Ev​≫kB​T are required for both species.

An increase of electrical conductivity due to light-generated mobile carriers. Generation, recombination, trapping and mobility determine the observable response.

Indium arsenide

Words: 35
Semiconductor OurBigBook.com
Indium arsenide, InAs, is a III-V semiconductor. An InAs island in a larger-gap host can provide quantum confinement for electrons and electron holes. The optical transition energy of a strained, confined island is not simply the bulk material's band gap.

Quantum dot

Words: 853 Articles: 17
Semiconductor OurBigBook.com
A quantum dot confines electrons and electron holes in all three spatial directions, producing discrete energy levels. A semiconductor island surrounded by a larger-band gap material is one realization. Its optical excitation and electron-hole recombination depend on confinement, Coulomb interactions and electric-dipole selection rules.

Electrostatically defined quantum dot

Words: 563 Articles: 11
Quantum dot OurBigBook.com
A small electron island confined laterally by depletion gates in an already vertically confined two-dimensional electron gas. Tunnel barriers couple it to reservoirs, and a plunger gate tunes charge occupation. Coulomb blockade and orbital confinement resolve individual electron additions.

Spin qubit in a gated quantum dot

Words: 40
Electrostatically defined quantum dot OurBigBook.com
A single confined electron's two spin states form a qubit when initialization, coherent rotations and measurement are controlled. Local driving rotates one spin; gate-controlled exchange can entangle neighboring dot spins. Spin-to-charge conversion permits electrical readout. Observing charge blockade alone does not demonstrate coherent qubit operation.

Double quantum dot

Words: 126 Articles: 2
Electrostatically defined quantum dot OurBigBook.com
Two capacitively and tunnel-coupled electron islands with separately tunable occupations. Detuning controls which dot holds an electron and whether two-electron charge states such as (1,1) and (0,2) are accessible.
Charge qubit in a double dot (H=(εσz​+2tc​σx​)/2)
Words: 48
Double quantum dot OurBigBook.com
A single electron shared by two dots has a left/right charge basis. In that basis, a two-level model is H=(εσz​+2tc​σx​)/2, where detuning sets the energy imbalance and tunnelling mixes the states. Electrical control and charge sensing are direct, but electric-potential fluctuations also couple strongly to the encoded information.
Exchange interaction in a double quantum dot (Hex​=Jσ1​⋅σ2​/4)
Words: 49
Double quantum dot OurBigBook.com
An effective coupling that separates the two-electron singlet state and triplet states by energy J. For a symmetric two-site Hubbard model with weak tunnelling tc​ and charging cost U, J≃4tc2​/U. Gate-controlled detuning and tunnelling change the interaction; the simple expression does not hold at arbitrary detuning or strong charge hybridization.

Spin-to-charge conversion

Words: 322 Articles: 5
Electrostatically defined quantum dot OurBigBook.com
A measurement method in which spin-dependent tunnelling or allowed charge transfer maps a spin outcome onto a distinguishable dot charge state. Quantum-dot charge sensing then records that charge. The measurement axis or singlet/triplet observable must be specified.
Tunnel-rate-selective spin readout
Words: 138 Articles: 1
Spin-to-charge conversion OurBigBook.com
Map states with unequal escape rates Γf​≫Γs​ onto distinct charge outcomes after an interval between their characteristic escape times. Both removal energies can lie above the reservoir chemical potential, so their splitting need not be thermally resolved. A useful rate difference must have a physical origin: a demonstrated single-dot example uses a two-electron singlet state and triplet state with different occupied orbitals. A bare single-electron Zeeman pair in the same orbital does not automatically provide the required rate contrast.[ref]
Optimal tunnel-rate readout time (τ∗​=log(Γf​/Γs​)/(Γf​−Γs​))
Words: 60
Tunnel-rate-selective spin readout OurBigBook.com
For independent exponential escape, equal prior probabilities and no state relaxation, the mean classification error is Pe​(τ)=[e−Γf​τ+1−e−Γs​τ]/2. Setting its derivative to zero gives the displayed interval. The error increases both when the fast state is not given enough time to escape and when the slow state is given too much. Detector bandwidth, relaxation and reloading require an expanded measurement model.
Pauli spin blockade
Words: 105 Articles: 1
Spin-to-charge conversion OurBigBook.com
Suppression of charge transfer by spin symmetry and the Pauli exclusion principle. For a double quantum dot, a (1,1) singlet state can enter the lowest (0,2) singlet, whereas a (1,1) triplet state is blocked if the required (0,2) triplet lies above the accessible energy window. Spin mixing or relaxation can lift blockade.
Magnetically driven spin-blockade lifting (hf=∣g∗∣μB​∣B0​∣)
Words: 61
Pauli spin blockade OurBigBook.com
A resonantly driven local electron-spin rotation can give a blocked two-dot triplet a singlet component, allowing spin-conserving charge transfer to a lowest-orbital doubly occupied dot. A common rotation of two perfectly identical spins does not mix singlet and triplet sectors, so relative spin rotation or an additional mixing mechanism is essential. Leakage-current spectroscopy tests resonant lifting; pulse-duration oscillations add evidence for coherent control.
Energy-selective spin readout
Words: 45
Spin-to-charge conversion OurBigBook.com
Place the reservoir chemical potential between the lower and higher Zeeman-split one-electron dot levels. The excited state can leave while the ground state remains trapped; a time-resolved charge sensor detects the temporary empty state. Thermal errors, missed fast tunnelling and relaxation before escape limit fidelity.

Quantum-dot charge sensing

Words: 40
Electrostatically defined quantum dot OurBigBook.com
Detection of a dot's charge through its capacitive influence on a nearby quantum point contact or single-electron transistor. Discrete charge changes shift the sensor response, allowing individual tunnel events to be resolved even when direct current through the dot is too small to measure.

Fock-Darwin spectrum (Enℓ​)

Words: 43
Quantum dot OurBigBook.com
For a circular two-dimensional parabolic dot in perpendicular magnetic field, orbital levels are ℏΩ(2n+∣ℓ∣+1)±ℓℏωc​/2, with Ω2=ω02​+ωc2​/4. The sign depends on the angular-momentum and signed-charge convention. At zero field the shell degeneracy is q+1 before spin; Zeeman and interaction terms require separate treatment.

Core-shell semiconductor nanocrystal

Words: 41
Quantum dot OurBigBook.com
A nanocrystal with one semiconducting composition surrounded by another. band offsets, interface quality and shell thickness govern carrier confinement and coupling to external traps. type-I band alignment favors electron and hole localization together; type-II band alignment can separate them. A larger shell band gap does not by itself determine those offsets.

Addition energy (Eadd​)

Words: 30
Quantum dot OurBigBook.com
The difference between successive electron-addition chemical potentials. In a constant interaction model it is Eadd​=e2/CΣ​+ϵN+1​−ϵN​, separating electrostatic charging from orbital level spacing. Spin, exchange and correlation can change the orbital contribution.

Quantum dot shell closure

Words: 50
Quantum dot OurBigBook.com
Filling a degenerate orbital shell produces a larger addition energy for the next electron. In a circular two-dimensional harmonic potential, shell q=nx​+ny​ has q+1 orbitals and capacity 2(q+1) including spin. Cumulative closed-shell occupancies are (q+1)(q+2)=2,6,12,20,…. Charging and orbital contributions must be separated, and anisotropy or exchange can split the ideal shells.

Self-assembled InAs quantum-dot single-photon source

Words: 96
Quantum dot OurBigBook.com
A quantum dot of InAs embedded in gallium arsenide confines injected electrons and electron holes. Strain-driven island formation supplies dots with lateral dimensions of order tens of nanometres and heights of a few nanometres. In an electrically driven implementation, a dot lies in a junction's intrinsic region. Selecting one dot spatially and one radiative line spectrally turns discrete exciton recombination into a single-photon source. Pulsed injection must avoid re-excitation during the same collection window.
The pioneering electrically driven device used an areal dot density around 5×108cm−2, a GaAs p-i-n structure and an aperture selecting individual-dot light.[ref]

Effective density of states (Nc​,Nv​)

Words: 52
Semiconductor OurBigBook.com
The effective density of states of a parabolic semiconductor band is its density of states integrated against a thermal Boltzmann factor measured from its edge. For one spin-degenerate valley,
Nc​=2(2πℏ2me∗​kB​T​)3/2,Nv​=2(2πℏ2mh∗​kB​T​)3/2.
(2)
These quantities have units of number per volume, unlike the energy-resolved density of states. In a nondegenerate semiconductor, n=Nc​e−(Ec​−μ)/(kB​T) and p=Nv​e−(μ−Ev​)/(kB​T); multiple equivalent valleys add their contributions.

Intrinsic semiconductor

Words: 452 Articles: 9
Semiconductor OurBigBook.com
An intrinsic semiconductor has equilibrium mobile electron and electron hole densities set predominantly by thermal excitation across its band gap, rather than by semiconductor doping. In the nondegenerate regime, charge neutrality gives n=p=ni​.

Constant-density-of-states intrinsic semiconductor (n=p=DkB​Tln(1+e−Eg​/(2kB​T)))

Words: 41
Intrinsic semiconductor OurBigBook.com
In a symmetric model with constant density of states D per volume and energy in two broad bands, charge neutrality gives μ=(Ec​+Ev​)/2 and n=p=DkB​Tln[1+e−Eg​/(2kB​T)]. In the nondegenerate limit, n≃DkB​Te−Eg​/(2kB​T). Thus the leading exponential activation law can coexist with an algebraic temperature prefactor.

Intrinsic Fermi level (Ei​)

Words: 22
Intrinsic semiconductor OurBigBook.com
The chemical potential fixed by equal conduction-electron and valence-hole densities in an intrinsic semiconductor. In the nondegenerate parabolic-band model, Ei​=(Ec​+Ev​)/2+(kB​T/2)ln(Nv​/Nc​).

Intrinsic-semiconductor chemical potential (μi​=(Ec​+Ev​)/2+(kB​T/2)ln(Nv​/Nc​))

Words: 47
Intrinsic semiconductor OurBigBook.com
For nondegenerate conduction bands and valence bands, charge neutrality gives Nc​e−(Ec​−μi​)/(kB​T)=Nv​e−(μi​−Ev​)/(kB​T). Taking logarithms yields
μi​=2Ec​+Ev​​+2kB​T​lnNc​Nv​​.
(3)
For single spin-degenerate parabolic extrema this becomes (Ec​+Ev​)/2+(3kB​T/4)ln(mh∗​/me∗​). Valley multiplicities or additional hole bands belong in Nc​,Nv​ and change the logarithm. The intrinsic chemical potential lies exactly at midgap only when the two effective density of states values agree.

Intrinsic carrier concentration (ni​)

Words: 315 Articles: 5
Intrinsic semiconductor OurBigBook.com
For nondegenerate bands separated by Eg​, the intrinsic carrier concentration is ni​=Nc​Nv​​e−Eg​/(2kB​T), using the effective density of states Nc​,Nv​. For fixed parabolic band effective masses and fixed gap, ni​∝T3/2e−Eg​/(2kB​T).

Intrinsic carrier extrapolation across a crossover

Words: 89
Intrinsic carrier concentration OurBigBook.com
In a nondegenerate parabolic-band semiconductor with fixed density-of-states mass, n(T)=CT3/2e−Δ(T)/(kB​T), where Δ(T)=Ec​(T)−μ(T). Thus
n(T1​)n(T2​)​=(T1​T2​​)3/2exp[−kB​T2​Δ(T2​)​+kB​T1​Δ(T1​)​].
(4)
A single measured value of Δ does not determine its temperature dependence. A fixed-gap intrinsic model instead has ni​=Ci​T3/2e−Eg​/(2kB​T), with the two effective density of states factors in Ci​. Identifying a crossover by ni​(Tc​)≃next​ gives an order-of-magnitude dopant-density estimate once that activation law is specified. At exact charge neutrality with ni​=next​, the total mobile-electron density is (1+5​)next​/2, so a crossover is not a sharp equality of every density definition.

Band-gap extraction from intrinsic carrier activation

Words: 68
Intrinsic carrier concentration OurBigBook.com
For fixed band effective masses and band gap Eg​, the intrinsic carrier concentration obeys ni​=CT3/2e−Eg​/(2kB​T). Thus
d(1/T)dln(ni​/T3/2)​=−2kB​Eg​​.
(5)
A base-ten plot against x=1000K/T instead has slope −Eg​/(2000kB​Kln10) after the prefactor correction. The intrinsic branch must be used, rather than the extrinsic plateau or dopant freeze-out branch. A changing gap or effective mass makes this an activation-energy estimate, and a small gap uncertainty can produce a much larger multiplicative uncertainty in a room-temperature minority density.

Semiconductor mass-action law (np=ni2​)

Words: 134 Articles: 2
Intrinsic carrier concentration OurBigBook.com
In thermal equilibrium, nondegenerate conduction electrons and valence electron holes share one chemical potential. Multiplying n=Nc​e−(Ec​−μ)/(kB​T) by p=Nv​e−(μ−Ev​)/(kB​T) cancels that chemical potential:
np=Nc​Nv​e−Eg​/(kB​T)=ni2​.
(6)
This relation remains valid with semiconductor doping under the stated assumptions. Equality of the two individual densities, n=p=ni​, additionally requires the intrinsic neutral case. Separate electron and hole quasi-Fermi levels in nonequilibrium need not obey this equilibrium product.
With one parabolic valley and two spin states at each band edge, the prefactor multiplying (kB​T)3 in the product is 4(mc​mh​)3/2/(2πℏ2)3. Both populations must be nondegenerate; the Pauli reduction of the pinned-edge mass-action product quantifies a failure of the classical approximation.
Pauli reduction of the pinned-edge mass-action product
Words: 41
Semiconductor mass-action law OurBigBook.com
For chemical potential at the conduction edge, divide the exact product by the classical prediction. The ratio is F1/2​(0)exF1/2​(−x), where x=Eg​/(kB​T). It is less than one, approaches F1/2​(0) as T→0, and approaches its square in the formal high-temperature parabolic model.
Spin and valley factors in the semiconductor mass-action constant
Semiconductor mass-action law OurBigBook.com

Homojunction

Words: 33
Semiconductor OurBigBook.com
A homojunction joins regions of the same semiconductor material with different semiconductor doping. Its bulk band gap is the same on both sides. This distinguishes the electrostatic band bending of a simple equilibrium p-n junction from the material-dependent band offsets possible in a heterojunction.

Wide-bandgap semiconductor

Words: 12
Semiconductor OurBigBook.com
A semiconductor with a comparatively large band gap; short-wavelength light-emitting diodes require sufficiently energetic optical transitions.

Nonradiative recombination

Words: 102 Articles: 2
Semiconductor OurBigBook.com
Electron-hole recombination that does not emit a photon; it competes with the radiative channel in a light-emitting diode.

Shockley-Read-Hall recombination

Words: 20
Nonradiative recombination OurBigBook.com
Trap-assisted recombination through defect states that capture electrons and holes sequentially. It can occur in the bulk or near interfaces.

Trap-assisted electron-hole recombination

Words: 67
Nonradiative recombination OurBigBook.com
A localized electronic defect can capture a conduction electron and subsequently an electron hole, or the reverse sequence, returning to its original charge state. Energy is transferred to the lattice rather than an emitted photon. The two-step process can remove an electron-hole pair even when direct band-to-band photon emission is inefficient. Its rate depends on trap density, occupation and both capture rates; a single trapping event is not necessarily completed recombination.

Acceptor impurity

Words: 95 Articles: 2
Semiconductor OurBigBook.com
An impurity that can accept an electron from the valence band, leaving a mobile hole. A shallow acceptor creates an impurity level in a crystal near and above the valence-band edge. Donor and acceptor levels are descriptions of appropriate dopants, not universal features of every impurity species.

Hydrogenic acceptor state (En​=−RA∗​/n2)

Words: 34
Acceptor impurity OurBigBook.com
A shallow acceptor can bind an electron hole through the screened Coulomb potential of a negatively charged impurity. A scalar band effective mass approximation gives a hydrogen-like bound-state ladder. Actual valence-band degeneracy and anisotropy can split levels and limit that approximation.

Hydrogen passivation of magnesium acceptors in gallium nitride

Words: 19
Acceptor impurity OurBigBook.com
In gallium nitride, incorporated hydrogen can neutralize magnesium acceptor impurities. Activation treatments restore electrical activity; adding magnesium alone does not establish a mobile electron hole population.

Donor impurity

Words: 275 Articles: 4
Semiconductor OurBigBook.com
An impurity that can supply an electron to the conduction band. A shallow donor has a localized occupied impurity level in a crystal near and below the conduction-band edge; thermal or other ionization releases its electron. The binding energy depends on the host dielectric response and effective mass.

Two-level donor occupancy (Pb​=[1+ge−Δ/(kB​T)]−1)

Words: 61
Donor impurity OurBigBook.com
A nondegenerate donor-bound state of energy zero and an excited representative conduction level of energy Δ>0 and degeneracy g have the displayed bound probability by canonical state counting. The inferred degeneracy from one measurement is g=(Pb−1​−1)eΔ/(kB​T). At finite fixed g, the probability decreases from1 toward 1/(1+g) as temperature grows. A temperature-independent effective degeneracy is an assumed two-level approximation; a full conduction-band density of states can behave differently.

Effective Bohr radius of a hydrogenic donor (aB∗​)

Words: 35
Donor impurity OurBigBook.com
In a scalar effective-mass dielectric model, the donor radius is aB∗​=ϵr​(me​/m∗)a0​. The effective mass reduces the kinetic-energy scale and dielectric screening weakens attraction. The corresponding binding energy scales as (m∗/me​)ϵr−2​ times the vacuum hydrogen binding energy.

Donor-state overlap estimate

Words: 68
Donor impurity OurBigBook.com
For shallow hydrogenic donor states of radius aB∗​ and random donor number density ND​, the mean spacing is of order ND−1/3​. Taking this spacing comparable to aB∗​ gives ND​∼(aB∗​)−3; a geometric diameter criterion instead gives ND​∼(2aB∗​)−3. The orbitals have exponentially decaying tails rather than hard boundaries, so there is no exact geometric onset. Appreciable overlap also limits the independent-donor ionisation model; a genuine transport transition needs additional electronic physics.

EB​=13.6057eVϵr2​m∗/me​​,aB∗​=a0​m∗/me​ϵr​​.
(7)
The donor level lies EB​ below the conduction band. These are magnitudes: the bound electron's energy relative to the band edge is negative. Band anisotropy, short-distance impurity structure and screening by mobile carriers can invalidate the simple Bohr model rescaling.

Mercury cadmium telluride is a semiconductor whose composition tunes its band gap and hence its long-wavelength absorption cutoff. It is widely used as the absorbing material in infrared detector arrays.

P-n junction

Words: 2k Articles: 14
Semiconductor OurBigBook.com
A p-n junction joins regions of a semiconductor with opposite majority charge carriers: electrons on one side and electron holes on the other. It provides the junction modeled by the Shockley diode equation.
Near an unbiased p-n junction, diffusion leaves exposed ionized donor impurities and acceptor impurities. Their electric field opposes further majority-carrier transfer. At thermal equilibrium, drift and diffusion balance; there is no net electric current. Forward bias reduces the barrier to carrier injection; reverse bias enlarges it. A heavily doped tunnel diode adds a different transport route, quantum tunnelling, that the ordinary Shockley diode equation omits.

Words: 188 Articles: 2
P-n junction OurBigBook.com
A linearly graded p-n junction has net ionized doping ND​−NA​=αx near the metallurgical junction. In the depletion approximation, ρ=eαx. With vanishing external field, neutrality places the depletion edges at ±w/2 and integration of Poisson equation gives
Ex​(x)=2εs​eα​(x2−4w2​).
(8)
The field points from n to p and has largest magnitude eαw2/(8εs​) at x=0. The potential is cubic inside the layer.

Words: 82
Linearly graded p-n junction OurBigBook.com
For a linearly graded p-n junction, the signed p-side depletion charge per area is Qp​=−eαw2/8. Differentiating with respect to positive p-side voltage V, using the linearly graded junction depletion width, gives the positive differential junction capacitance per area
CA​=dVdQp​​=wεs​​=[12(Vb​−V)eαεs2​​]1/3.
(9)
Thus CA−3​ is linear in V. If stored charge denotes the positive n-side magnitude Qn​=−Qp​, its derivative with respect to V is negative; the positive capacitance is instead −dQn​/dV=dQn​/dVR​ for reverse-voltage magnitude VR​=−V. Neither definition uses the zero net charge of the whole depletion layer.

Integrating the electric field across a linearly graded p-n junction gives Vb​−V=eαw3/(12εs​), where positive V means forward bias. Thus the depletion region width depends on the cube root of the remaining barrier voltage. Both the space-charge density and integration range grow with width; this differs from the square-root width law of an abrupt uniformly doped junction.

Built-in potential (Vb​)

Words: 63
P-n junction OurBigBook.com
The built-in potential of a p-n junction is the electrostatic potential difference established when carrier diffusion exposes ionized dopants until the opposing drift and diffusion currents balance. The equilibrium electrochemical potential is constant even though the electric potential and band edges vary. In a nondegenerate homojunction with neutral-edge majority densities pp​,nn​, eVb​=kB​Tlog(pp​nn​/ni2​). This is band bending within the same material, not necessarily a discontinuous offset of different materials' band edges.

Tunnel diode

Words: 1k Articles: 2
P-n junction OurBigBook.com
A tunnel diode is a p-n junction with sufficiently heavy semiconductor doping on both sides to make a thin depletion region and permit substantial interband tunnelling. The neutral regions are degenerate semiconductors. Its distinctive forward current-voltage characteristic contains a peak followed by a valley: over part of the curve, increasing the applied electric potential difference decreases the electric current. The Esaki tunnel-diode experiment made this behavior experimentally concrete.
The useful quantity is the local slope, not the ratio of total voltage to total electric current. With conventional electric current I entering the positive-voltage terminal, define
gd​=dVdI​,rd​=dIdV​=gd​1​(gd​=0).
(10)
Negative differential resistance means gd​<0, hence rd​<0 where defined. A forward operating point can still have V>0, I>0 and absorbed power VI>0. A small voltage increase then gives a negative current increment; this does not make the total electric current negative or turn the device into an unlimited source of energy. The external supply sets the operating point and supplies the energy available for an electronic amplifier.
An original idealized construction explains the shape. Put the n-type semiconductor on the left and the p-type semiconductor on the right. Take q>0 as the elementary charge and V=Vp​−Vn​. Increasing forward bias lowers the right-hand electron energy levels relative to the left. Denote the two reservoir electrochemical potentials by μn​,μp​, so that μn​−μp​=qV. At zero temperature, occupied left-hand conduction band states extend up to μn​; empty right-hand valence band states start at μp​. For transfer conserving electron energy, the available interval is
max(Ec,n​,μp​)<E<min(μn​,Ev,p​).
(11)
It is nonempty only when its upper endpoint exceeds its lower endpoint. Both an occupied initial quantum state and an empty final quantum state must exist at the same energy. The Pauli exclusion principle prevents transfer into an already occupied final quantum state.
For the original diagram, choose arbitrary energy units with Ec,n​=−0.5, μn​=0, μp​=−u and Ev,p​=0.5−u, where u is qV in those units. The available interval has width
L(u)=max(0,min(0,0.5−u)−max(−0.5,−u)),u≥0.
(12)
Thus L(0.25)=0.25, L(0.50)=0.50, L(0.70)=0.30, and L(1.15)=0. Initially forward bias opens a transfer window; further forward bias closes it by moving the right-hand valence band edge below the left-hand conduction band edge. This is a state-counting illustration, not a formula for a measured electric current.
For reverse bias, the transfer direction changes: occupied right-hand valence band states can feed empty left-hand conduction band states. In the same construction, u=−0.70 opens the interval 0<E<0.70 for this reverse transfer. A narrow depletion region allows a large reverse quantum tunnelling electric current at small electric potential difference, whereas the ordinary Shockley diode equation predicts only a small reverse saturation electric current before diode reverse breakdown. At zero biasing, equal reservoir occupations give zero net electric current; quantum tunnelling does not require a net equilibrium flow.
A finite-temperature refinement replaces sharp occupation cutoffs with the Fermi-Dirac distribution. An illustrative weak-transfer expression is
In→p​(V)=K∫W(E,V)[fn​(E)−fp​(E)]dE,K>0.
(13)
Here W≥0 describes allowed initial/final quantum states and their coupling, and fn​,fp​ are Fermi-Dirac distributions with the respective electrochemical potentials. The occupation difference follows by subtracting the reverse transfer factor from the forward one: fn​(1−fp​)−fp​(1−fn​)=fn​−fp​. An overlap interval alone does not determine W: transmission probability, density of states, crystal momentum selection and phonons can matter. A complete germanium calculation is more demanding than multiplying two constant density of states factors. At larger forward bias, ordinary carrier injection and diffusion supply a rising current branch even after direct band overlap is lost.

Esaki tunnel-diode experiment (1957–1958)

Words: 280
Tunnel diode OurBigBook.com
Leo Esaki's 1958 report describes alloy-fabricated germanium p-n junctions, with acceptor impurity concentration 1.6×1019cm−3 and donor impurity concentration approximately 1019cm−3. Its readout was the current-voltage characteristic: a forward peak occurred at 0.035±0.005V. The report says specimens could be reproduced; above 0.3V the forward branch approximately followed the ordinary Shockley diode equation.[ref]
In his 1973 lecture, Leo Esaki recalls an earlier junction whose strong room-temperature reverse conduction preceded a negative-slope forward segment revealed by cooling. Its estimated zero-bias width was about 200 ångströms (20nm), supported by capacitance measurements. Increasing semiconductor doping further made the negative slope visible across the measured temperatures, including room temperature. Thus preparation and temperature variation were experimental controls, not merely changes to a theoretical diagram. The low onset voltage argued against avalanche production of electrons and electron holes; the energy band explanation connected the forward decline to loss of available final states.[ref]
The historical readouts were junction electric current versus applied electric potential difference and a separate capacitance check; preparation and temperature were varied. The cited descriptions do not identify a meter model or give a complete wiring diagram.
For a modern repetition, measure junction voltage directly while stepping the supply and recording electric current, repeat both sweep directions, and compare temperatures and differently doped specimens. These are proposed controls, not a reconstruction of the historical apparatus. Lead electrical resistance, Joule heating, contact quality and voltage resolution can obscure the result. The tunnel-diode load-line stability calculation also predicts that an external resistor can make a negative-slope operating point inaccessible in a slow sweep. A jump in terminal readings then need not mean the underlying current-voltage characteristic is discontinuous.

Tunnel-diode load-line stability (1/R+I′(V)>0)

Words: 447
Tunnel diode OurBigBook.com
A current-voltage characteristic determines possible steady operating points; it does not alone determine their linear stability. Consider an ideal voltage source Vs​ feeding a tunnel diode through a resistor R>0, with a positive constant capacitance C across the junction. Assume a quasistatic device relation I(V) and neglect inductance, transit delays, noise and heating. Kirchhoff's current law gives the original one-state model
CV˙=RVs​−V​−I(V).
(14)
A steady operating point V∗​ satisfies I(V∗​)=(Vs​−V∗​)/R: the device curve intersects the descending supply line. This is the source-side counterpart of a resistive load line. A small perturbation V=V∗​+δV obeys
CδV˙=−(R1​+I′(V∗​))δV,λ=−C1/R+I′(V∗​)​.
(15)
Thus the equilibrium point is locally attracting if 1/R+I′(V∗​)>0 and unstable if the inequality reverses. Equality requires higher-order analysis. Even on a negative differential resistance segment, a sufficiently small supply electrical resistance can stabilize this model. The assumption about the electrical circuit matters: an inductive or delayed circuit has additional state variables and may behave differently.
Choose an original toy forward characteristic, with no fitted device parameters:
x=V0​V​,I(V)=I0​i(x),i(x)=x3−6x2+10x=x((x−3)2+1),
(16)
where V0​=0.10V, I0​=1.0mA and 0≤x≤3.6. For every x>0, i(x)>0, so this entire forward curve absorbs positive total power. Nevertheless
I′(V)=V0​I0​​(3x2−12x+10)<0⟺2−36​​<x<2+36​​.
(17)
The model therefore separates negative differential resistance from negative total V/I. The corresponding peak and valley are at approximately 0.1184V and 0.2816V; these voltages deliberately differ from the historical peak.
With R=100Ω and Vs​=0.60V, the supply line is I/I0​=6−x. The intersection equation factors exactly:
i(x)+x−6=(x−1)(x−2)(x−3)=0.
(18)
The three operating points are (0.10V,5mA), (0.20V,4mA) and (0.30V,3mA). Their values of 1/R+I′(V∗​) are respectively 20, −10 and 20mS. The outer two attract nearby trajectories; the middle one repels them. This is bistability in the specified one-state electrical circuit.
For the second panel, choose R=25Ω and Vs​=0.30V. Now I/I0​=12−4x and
i(x)+4x−12=(x−2)((x−2)2+2)=0.
(19)
There is exactly one real operating point, again (0.20V,4mA). Here 1/R+I′(V∗​)=20mS>0, despite the device's own slope I′(V∗​)=−20mS. With C=10nF, the perturbation decays with time constant C/(20mS)=0.50μs; the unstable middle point of the first panel has growth time 1.0μs.
The one-state autonomous model supports switching between attracting operating points after a perturbation or parameter change; it cannot produce a nonconstant periodic orbit. A proposed oscillator needs additional dynamics. This limitation is useful: a load-line intersection establishes a possible steady reading, the slope test establishes local attraction in a specified model, and neither calculation alone predicts an oscillation frequency for a real tunnel diode.

The region around a p-n junction with reduced mobile charge carrier density.
An illustrative abrupt-junction depletion approximation assumes uniform, fully ionized donor impurities and acceptor impurities, negligible mobile space charge in the depleted layer, and permittivity εs​. For area A, doping number densities NA​,ND​ and built-in electric potential difference Vbi​, it gives
W≃q2εs​​(NA​1​+ND​1​)(Vbi​−V)​,Cj​≃Wεs​A​.

Here q>0 is the elementary charge and V is positive for forward bias. Increasing both doping densities reduces W in this estimate. That explains the preparation strategy for a tunnel diode; it does not make this sharp-depletion approximation a precise microscopic model of a degenerate semiconductor.

Depletion region OurBigBook.com
Thermal generation of electron-hole pairs within a reverse-biased depletion region can supply a leakage electric current in addition to neutral-region diffusion. For a simple midgap trap with equal electron and hole lifetime parameters, its scale is eAWni​/(2τg​), where W is depletion width and τg​ the lifetime parameter. The electric field separates generated carriers. Unlike ideal diode minority-carrier diffusion current, this contribution scales approximately with ni​ rather than ni2​ and can vary with reverse voltage through W. Consequently a measured activation energy need not equal the full band gap.

Depletion region OurBigBook.com
The depletion approximation replaces the junction's transition region by a region without mobile carriers, leaving only fixed ionized dopants. For a uniformly doped abrupt p-n junction, ρ=−eNA​ on the p side, ρ=+eND​ on the n side and ρ≃0 outside. Charge neutrality gives NA​xp​=ND​xn​. Integrating Poisson equation gives the electric field and the electrostatic band bending.

Depletion approximation OurBigBook.com
For a planar abrupt p-n junction with ionized densities NA​,ND​, p-side width wp​ and n-side width wn​, zero external field requires NA​wp​=ND​wn​. Integrating Poisson equation gives Vbi​−V=e(NA​wp2​+ND​wn2​)/(2εs​), with positive V denoting forward bias. Therefore W=wn​+wp​ has the displayed value, wn​=NA​W/(NA​+ND​) and wp​=ND​W/(NA​+ND​). The positive depletion capacitance per area is CA​=εs​/W. It equals dQp​/dV=−dQn​/dV when Qp​=−eNA​wp​ and Qn​=eND​wn​ are signed space charges per area. Differentiating a positive charge magnitude with respect to forward voltage instead gives a negative derivative. The square-root law assumes partially depleted regions, negligible mobile charge and no substantial injected-carrier storage.

For a zero-bias abrupt p-n junction, choose the p side at x<0 and the n side at x>0. Ionized acceptors and donors remain fixed while mobile electrons and electron holes diffuse and establish a built-in electric field. In the depletion approximation, mobile carriers are neglected on −xp​<x<xn​ and the net charge density is
ρ(x)=⎩⎨⎧​−eNA​,+eND​,0,​−xp​<x<0,0<x<xn​,outside the depletion region.​

Charge neutrality gives NA​xp​=ND​xn​. The quasi-neutral bulk can have a large mobile carrier density while its net charge density is nearly zero, because fixed dopant charge compensates it. With complete ionization and nondegenerate carriers, equilibrium also gives np=ni2​; real carrier profiles vary smoothly rather than forming exact step functions at depletion edges.

Depletion region OurBigBook.com
The incremental capacitance associated with changes of electric charge around a p-n junction. Its depletion contribution is often estimated by Cj​≃εs​A/W, so an independent junction capacitance measurement can constrain the width W of the depletion region under the model assumptions. Other stored electric charge, including injected minority carriers, can also contribute to a measured terminal capacitance.

Junction capacitance OurBigBook.com
Let each side of a symmetric abrupt p-n junction have thickness d, area A and doping density N. Partial depletion gives w2=εs​(Vbi​−V)/(eN). Both sides become fully depleted at Vfd​=Vbi​−eNd2/εs​. Beyond that point, the ionized dopant charges are fixed, but an incremental terminal voltage changes the electric field uniformly across the full thickness 2d. Gauss's law then gives dQterminal​=εs​AdV/(2d), up to terminal orientation. The measured positive capacitance approaches Cfd​ rather than vanishing. This geometrical result assumes ideal contacts, negligible mobile carriers, no breakdown and no other series capacitances.

Semiconductor OurBigBook.com
The controlled introduction of impurities to change a semiconductor's charge carrier populations. Donor impurities and acceptor impurities can produce an n-type semiconductor or a p-type semiconductor, respectively; compensation and temperature also matter.

Before using a Maxwell–Boltzmann chemical-potential formula in a doped semiconductor, compare the carrier density to its conduction-band effective density of states. When n is much larger than Nc​, a nondegenerate logarithmic estimate is inconsistent. Use Fermi–Dirac statistics or a controlled degenerate expansion instead. A small effective mass strongly reduces Nc​ and raises the Fermi energy at fixed density, so even an otherwise familiar donor concentration can put the chemical potential inside the conduction band.

Semiconductor doping OurBigBook.com
At sufficiently low temperature, thermal ionization of shallow dopants becomes inefficient, reducing the mobile carrier density. An acceptor-doped sample may then have many neutral acceptors and few mobile electron holes. Extracting an activation energy requires a model of dopant ionization and compensation; the mobile density need not have the same simple activation exponent in every compensation regime.

Introduction of dopants by accelerating ions into a solid. Their depth distribution, lattice damage and electrical activation depend on implantation and subsequent annealing.

Placing dopants away from the carrier channel to reduce ionized-impurity scattering while supplying carriers.

A two-dimensional electron gas supplied by remote donors in aluminium gallium arsenide and confined on the gallium arsenide side of a heterojunction. A compensated semiconductor contains both donor impurities and acceptor impurities. In a nondegenerate equilibrium model with both species fully ionized, charge neutrality gives n−p=Δ=ND​−NA​, while the semiconductor semiconductor mass-action law gives np=ni2​. Solving yields
n=2Δ+Δ2+4ni2​​​,p=2−Δ+Δ2+4ni2​​​.
(22)
For Δ>0 and ni​≪Δ, n≃Δ and p≃ni2​/Δ. Numerically the minority concentration is better obtained as ni2​/n than by subtracting nearly equal numbers. If dopants are only partly ionized, replace ND​,NA​ in charge neutrality by their ionized concentrations and determine the chemical potential self-consistently.

An amphoteric dopant can act as a donor impurity or an acceptor impurity according to its incorporated lattice site or defect configuration. Silicon in gallium arsenide is the standard example: substitution on the gallium sublattice gives a shallow donor, while substitution on the arsenic sublattice gives a shallow acceptor. Its electrical effect therefore depends on growth conditions as well as total silicon concentration.[ref]

Its ionized fraction is therefore ND+​/ND​=[1+2e(EF​−ED​)/(kB​T)]−1. The conduction-band relation n=Nc​e(EF​−Ec​)/(kB​T) gives ND+​=ND​/[1+(2n/Nc​)eEb​/(kB​T)]. Its left side increases strictly for n>0 and its right side decreases, so there is one physical solution, with n≥ni​. If donor orbit radii greatly exceed their separation, an independent isolated-hydrogenic-level model itself fails and overlapping impurity states or band reconstruction are needed. Semiconductor doping OurBigBook.com
Substitutional semiconductor doping replaces selected host atoms with impurity atoms on ordinary lattice sites. A shallow donor impurity can supply a mobile conduction electron and remain positively charged; a shallow acceptor impurity can capture an electron and leave a mobile valence hole, remaining negatively charged. In nondegenerate, substantially ionized material, donor-dominated doping raises the chemical potential toward the conduction edge and acceptor-dominated doping lowers it toward the valence edge. Dopants do not create net bulk charge in a neutral sample: fixed impurity charge compensates the mobile carrier charge. Freeze-out, compensation and degeneracy qualify the simplest relation between dopant and carrier densities.

Carriers remain bound to dopants rather than contributing to conduction, reducing the mobile carrier density. This dopant freeze-out is distinct from the high-temperature intrinsic regime, where thermal excitation across the band gap overwhelms the net dopant contribution.

A shallow donor impurity introduces a level just below the conduction band, and a shallow acceptor impurity introduces one just above the valence band. Under electrostatic band bending, these levels shift with the local band edges in the same material; their occupation is determined relative to the equilibrium chemical potential.

The occupied and empty quantum states on opposite sides of a tunnel diode can then overlap in energy. Heavy semiconductor doping both changes these occupations and narrows the depletion region; a narrow barrier and accessible final quantum states serve different roles.

Field-effect transistor OurBigBook.com
A transistor whose active semiconductor channel is a thin film on a supporting substrate. Semiconductor purity, channel continuity, gate dielectric and contacts jointly determine switching; a high intrinsic charge carrier mobility alone does not guarantee a uniform transistor array.

Junction field-effect transistor

Words: 155 Articles: 1
Field-effect transistor OurBigBook.com
A junction field-effect transistor controls a conducting semiconductor channel using reverse-biased p-n junctions at its gate. Changing gate voltage changes the depletion region and therefore the cross-section available to mobile charge carriers. A depletion-mode n-channel device normally conducts at zero gate-source voltage and is depleted by a more negative gate. The small reverse gate electric current gives high input resistance, while a source-drain supply provides output power.
Pinch-off in a junction field-effect transistor
Words: 99
Junction field-effect transistor OurBigBook.com
In an n-channel junction field-effect transistor, increasing drain voltage increases the local gate-channel reverse bias near the drain. The depletion region can meet there, ending the quasi-neutral channel before the drain. Carriers already in the channel are swept across the remaining high-field region, so drain-end pinch-off produces current saturation rather than zero current. A sufficiently negative gate voltage can instead deplete the whole channel and cut the device off. In the one-sided depletion approximation, a channel half-width a and donor density ND​ give a depletion threshold voltage UP​=eND​a2/(2εs​); with built-in junction voltage Vbi​, drain-end pinch-off occurs approximately at VDS​=UP​−Vbi​+VGS​.

MOSFET

Words: 240 Articles: 4
Field-effect transistor OurBigBook.com
A metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor, with an insulating layer separating the gate from the semiconductor. Its gate electric field controls the channel's mobile charge carriers; a semiconductor inversion layer can form a two-dimensional electron gas.
Long-channel MOSFET current law (ID​=μCox​(W/L)[(VGS​−VT​)VDS​−VDS2​/2])
Words: 94
MOSFET OurBigBook.com
For an n-channel MOSFET, assume a gradual channel, constant charge carrier mobility μ, gate capacitance per area Cox​, width W and length L. With overdrive Vov​=VGS​−VT​>0, the inversion-sheet charge magnitude is Cox​(Vov​−V(x)). The drift-current relation ID​=μWCox​(Vov​−V)V′ is constant along the channel. Integrating from V=0 to VDS​ over length L proves the displayed expression for 0≤VDS​≤Vov​. At the drain pinch-off condition VDS​=Vov​, it yields ID,sat​=μCox​WVov2​/(2L). This ideal saturation neglects channel-length modulation and short-channel velocity saturation.
Gate-to-substrate Fermi-level difference (μ​g​−μ​s​=−eVg​)
Words: 71
MOSFET OurBigBook.com
An ideal insulating gate blocks particle exchange between the gate and substrate of a MOSFET. Their electrochemical potentials, represented by their band-diagram Fermi levels, therefore need not coincide. An applied gate voltage fixes their difference; with e>0 and voltage defined by an electron reservoir, μ​g​−μ​s​=−eVg​. Contact work-function differences also affect band bending, so equal Fermi levels do not imply flat bands. Each conducting region can separately have a spatially constant equilibrium electrochemical potential.
CMOS
Words: 50 Articles: 1
MOSFET OurBigBook.com
An integrated circuit technology using complementary MOSFETs. CMOS names a circuit technology; active-pixel sensor names a detector architecture.
CMOS inverter
Words: 37
CMOS OurBigBook.com
A complementary p-channel/n-channel transistor pair with joined gates as input and joined drains as output. The p-channel device pulls toward the positive supply and the n-channel device toward ground, producing logic inversion with ideally zero settled-state through-current.

Point-contact transistor

Words: 403 Articles: 1
Transistor OurBigBook.com
A point-contact transistor has two closely spaced rectifying contacts, the emitter and collector, and a third low-electrical resistance base contact to the semiconductor. The Bardeen-Brattain point-contact transistor experiment established amplification using this arrangement. It does not require two fabricated bulk p-n junctions.

Bardeen-Brattain point-contact transistor experiment (1947)

Words: 369
Point-contact transistor OurBigBook.com
In December 1947, John Bardeen and Walter Houser Brattain obtained transistor action at Bell Telephone Laboratories. William Shockley proposed the distinct bipolar junction transistor within the following month.[ref]
Their 1948 paper describes ground, etched germanium, initially also anodized and rinsed. Surface contacts separated by 50–250μm share a broad base contact. Positive emitter biasing injects electron holes; negative collector biasing draws them toward the collector. An input signal changes emitter electric current, and a collector electrical load converts the resulting change into voltage.[ref]
Early electric field control experiments gave unexpectedly weak responses. John Bardeen proposed that surface states screened the interior. Surface charge could create a barrier and a hole-rich semiconductor inversion layer. Replacing an electrolyte control with a gold contact reversed the response sign, suggesting electron hole carrier injection. Closely spaced contacts made from a gold-coated wedge split with a razor then enabled power gain. The relative importance of surface and bulk transport depended on preparation and collector forming.[ref]
The 1948 authors found that collector-current increments could exceed emitter-current increments; their current gain depended on biasing.[ref] A terminal-current ratio alone cannot identify the microscopic path. Surface states, the local barrier, carrier injection and contact preparation prevent a single ideal modern bipolar junction transistor model from explaining every point-contact transistor.
For the conventional electric current directions drawn in the figure, IE​ enters the emitter, IC​ leaves the collector and signed IB​ enters the base. Kirchhoff's current law requires
IE​+IB​=IC​,α=(∂IE​∂IC​​)VC​​,δIB​=(α−1)δIE​at fixed VC​.
(24)
Thus a local current gain α>1 requires an accompanying base-current change. The collector increment is not simply a count of injected electron holes, and it does not violate electric charge conservation.
For an experiment following the functional arrangement, first establish each contact's separate current-voltage characteristic relative to the base. Then hold collector biasing fixed, vary a small emitter signal, and compare the collector electrical load voltage with the input. A decisive power gain check measures both input electric current and voltage and the output power in a known electrical load; voltage enlargement alone is insufficient. These are proposed measurement controls, not additional claims about the 1947 laboratory record.
Repeating a setting tests drift; reversing or removing emitter biasing tests whether the response requires carrier injection. Contact motion, surface contamination, temperature, direct electrical coupling and noise can all affect the inference. A small-signal model describes measured local terminal response without deciding every microscopic mechanism.

Bipolar junction transistor

Words: 96 Articles: 1
Transistor OurBigBook.com
A bipolar junction transistor has two p-n junctions sharing a thin base region, arranged n-p-n or p-n-p. In its forward amplification regime, the emitter junction injects minority carriers; many cross the base before electron-hole recombination and reach the reverse-biased collector junction.[ref]

Shockley junction transistor proposal

Words: 58
Bipolar junction transistor OurBigBook.com
William Shockley's proposal used transport through the bulk of a semiconductor, rather than coupling between two surface points. The base must be thin enough for injected minority carriers to reach the collector. Two separately wired diodes do not supply that shared transport region. The proposal was a design principle; producing a working device required further control of material properties.[ref]

Transistor small-signal amplifier (Av​=−gm​(RD​∥ro​∥RL​))

Words: 507
Transistor OurBigBook.com
An original teaching model exposes the roles of input loading, output loading and the supply. Choose a small-signal model with positive input electrical resistance ri​, transconductance gm​>0, and output electrical resistance ro​>0. Its controlled output current source draws gm​vi​ from the output node toward the reference node. This chosen sign gives an inverting voltage gain; it is not the historical contact circuit's sign convention.
Assume a fixed operating point, negligible reverse coupling, a frequency range where coupling capacitors pass the signal, and negligible other capacitances and transit delays. A collector resistor RD​ connects the output to a steady ideal supply VDD​; an external electrical load RL​ is coupled through a capacitor, so it draws no direct current. The input source has series electrical resistance Rs​. All voltages below are small departures from the operating point. An ideal fixed supply has zero incremental voltage and therefore becomes the reference node in the small-signal model.
Define RO​=RD​∥ro​ and RP​=RO​∥RL​, where a∥b=ab/(a+b). Input voltage division and output Kirchhoff's current law give
vi​=Rs​+ri​ri​​vs​,RD​vo​​+ro​vo​​+RL​vo​​+gm​vi​=0.
(25)
Consequently the port voltage gain, overall source-to-output voltage gain, and load current gain magnitudes are
Av​=vi​vo​​=−gm​RP​,vs​vo​​=−gm​RP​Rs​+ri​ri​​,∣Ai​∣=∣vi​∣/ri​∣vo​∣/RL​​=gm​ri​RO​+RL​RO​​.
(26)
This current gain uses load electric current, not all the controlled-source electric current. It is also a different port definition from the historical emitter-to-collector current gain. Larger Rs​ attenuates the input; smaller RL​ attenuates the output.
For a sinusoid input signal, use root mean square voltages. The power gain from accepted input signal power Pi​=vi2​/ri​ to useful load power PL​=vo2​/RL​ is
GP​=Pi​PL​​=gm2​ri​(RO​+RL​)2RO2​RL​​.
(27)
Unlike ∣Ai​∣, this tends to zero as either RL​→0 or RL​→∞. Differentiation gives
dRL​dGP​​=gm2​ri​RO2​(RO​+RL​)3RO​−RL​​,GP,max​=4gm2​ri​RO​​at RL​=RO​.
(28)
Thus matching the output electrical load maximizes delivered power in this unilateral resistive model. For fixed source voltage, input loading multiplies PL​ by [ri​/(Rs​+ri​)]2; the accepted-input power gain above excludes the loss in Rs​.
Choose ri​=Rs​=1kΩ, gm​=2mS, ro​=20kΩ, and RD​=2kΩ. Then RO​=20/11kΩ. With RL​=2kΩ and vs​=20mV root mean square, the input is 10mV and the inverted output has magnitude 19.0476mV root mean square. Hence Pi​=0.100μW and PL​=0.181406μW: GP​=1.81406. These are calculated values of the chosen model, not historical measurements.
With the same parameters but RL​=100Ω, ∣Ai​∣=1.89573 while GP​=0.359381<1. At RL​=10kΩ, ∣Av​∣=3.07692 while GP​=0.946746<1. Neither current gain nor voltage gain alone establishes power gain.
For the direct current load line in the figure, choose VDD​=6V, IQ​=1mA and VQ​=4V, consistent with VQ​=VDD​−RD​IQ​. Locally extend the model as I=IQ​+gm​vi​+(V−VQ​)/ro​. With the external electrical load isolated at direct current, its intersection with I=(VDD​−V)/RD​ is V=VQ​−gm​RO​vi​. Keeping ∣vo​∣ small compared with the available voltage headroom is essential; extrapolation to arbitrarily large signals would be unphysical.
At the chosen operating point the collector supply delivers VDD​IQ​=6mW: 2mW is dissipated in RD​ and 4mW in the output device. Under a small signal, that energy flow is redistributed to provide load power. The incremental controlled current source hides the supply's steady energy flow; it does not create energy. A real complete amplifier also needs its input biasing network and has further losses. This calculation establishes neither its total efficiency nor a universal law for point-contact transistors.

Semiconductor OurBigBook.com Tags: Electrical circuit

High-electron-mobility transistor

Words: 17
Semiconductor device OurBigBook.com
A heterostructure transistor with a high-mobility channel spatially separated from ionized dopants; the gate modulates channel population.

Semiconductor heterostructure

Words: 1k Articles: 16
Semiconductor OurBigBook.com
A semiconductor heterostructure combines different semiconductors, using their interfaces and spatially varying band gaps to control device behavior.[ref]

Lattice mismatch

Words: 17
Semiconductor heterostructure OurBigBook.com
A difference between the in-plane lattice spacings of joined crystals, which can cause strain and crystal defects during epitaxy.

Epitaxial buffer layer

Words: 20
Semiconductor heterostructure OurBigBook.com
An intermediate layer used to prepare the growth of a later layer by epitaxy; it need not eliminate the lattice mismatch.

Heterojunction

Words: 227 Articles: 3
Semiconductor heterostructure OurBigBook.com
A heterojunction joins different semiconductors; its two sides need not have opposite semiconductor doping.[ref]

Type-II band alignment

Words: 37
Heterojunction OurBigBook.com
A staggered alignment in which the lowest electron states and most favorable hole states occur in different materials. Unlike type-I band alignment, it can reduce electron–hole spatial overlap. Comparing the two band gaps alone does not determine whether this alignment occurs.

Band offset (ΔEc​,ΔEv​)

Words: 95
Heterojunction OurBigBook.com
A band offset is an interface discontinuity in a conduction band or valence band edge.[ref]
For a chosen two-material example, let the central material A have Ec,A​=1 and Ev,A​=0, and the surrounding material B have Ec,B​=1.6 and Ev,B​=−0.4, in stipulated energy units. Define positive confinement barriers by ΔEc​=Ec,B​−Ec,A​ and ΔEv​=Ev,A​−Ev,B​. Then ΔEc​=0.6, ΔEv​=0.4, and the band gaps obey
Eg,B​−Eg,A​=ΔEc​+ΔEv​=1.
(29)
This identity determines the sum of the band offsets; a band gap difference alone cannot determine their partition. The chosen numbers illustrate the definition and do not specify a measured material pair.

Type-I band alignment

Words: 80
Heterojunction OurBigBook.com
A type-I band alignment confines electrons and electron holes together: its inner conduction band edge is lower, its valence band edge higher.[ref]
In the chosen band offset example, the electron barrier is 0.6, while the electron hole barrier is 0.4. A hole's excitation energy is measured downward from a valence band maximum: reversing that convention would incorrectly make the two barriers appear to repel opposite carriers. An electrostatic shift −qϕ moves both electron energy band edges together; changing the band gap also changes their separation. Thus material composition supplies a control beyond the electric potential ϕ alone.

Double heterostructure

Words: 422 Articles: 2
Semiconductor heterostructure OurBigBook.com
A double heterostructure sandwiches one semiconductor between two layers of another, for example gallium arsenide between aluminium gallium arsenide layers. Suitable band offsets confine injected charge carriers centrally.[ref]

Double heterostructure laser

Words: 401 Articles: 1
Double heterostructure OurBigBook.com
A double heterostructure laser electrically pumps its central layer for stimulated emission. Band offsets confine charge carriers; refractive index contrast confines the optical normal mode.[ref]
For an original bookkeeping model, let R be the injected pair rate per unit area, d the active-layer thickness, N its excess pair number density, τ a recombination lifetime, and τe​ an escape time. Before appreciable stimulated emission, suppose
dtdN​=dR​−τN​−τe​N​,Nss​=dRτ​1+τ/τe​1​.
(30)
Choose two otherwise identical devices with τe​=τ and τe​=9τ. The resulting steady state populations are Rτ/(2d) and 9Rτ/(10d): improved confinement raises the population by a factor 1.8 at fixed injection. This linear model assumes equal excess electron and electron hole densities, fixed lifetimes, and no laser gain clamping.
Optical confinement enters separately. For a chosen optical normal mode, define 0<Γ≤1 as its gain-overlap factor with the active layer. With material optical gain g, internal loss αi​, and mirror loss αm​, a simple laser threshold condition is
Γg=αi​+αm​.
(31)
For stipulated losses αi​+αm​=3 in inverse-length units, Γ=1/2 requires g=6, whereas Γ=3/4 requires g=4. This calculation varies optical overlap only; the preceding population calculation varies carrier escape only. Their combination explains the usefulness of controlling both the energy band profile and the optical normal mode.
Herbert Kroemer proposed the double heterostructure laser in 1963; he did not participate in its 1970 experimental realization.[ref] Zhores I. Alferov describes his group's independent 1963 proposal and later experimental program.[ref]
Continuous double heterostructure laser experiment
Words: 146
Double heterostructure laser OurBigBook.com
The experimental distinction is concrete. A 1962 gallium arsenide p-n junction laser used top and bottom contacts, parallel polished faces, and current pulses with the device in liquid nitrogen. An infrared image converter recorded the radiation pattern; a spectrometer measured narrowing above laser threshold. Comparing the same device below and above laser threshold supplied a control. Pulsed, cooled operation did not demonstrate continuous operation at room temperature.[ref]
Zhores I. Alferov's 1970 team photolithographically patterned stripe double heterostructure lasers on silver-covered copper plates. He reports sustained laser emission at room temperature; Fig. 4 shows the device structure. Independently, Izuo Hayashi, Morton B. Panish and collaborators demonstrated continuous double heterostructure laser operation with diamond heat sinks.[ref]
The below-threshold comparison tests the onset of stimulated emission; continuous operation additionally requires sustained removal of waste heat. Neither observation alone measures the separate band offsets, optical overlap, or every loss mechanism. The schematic above therefore explains a design principle rather than reconstructing the historical apparatus.

Quantum well

Words: 589 Articles: 6
Semiconductor heterostructure OurBigBook.com
A quantum well confines a particle in one spatial direction while allowing motion along the layer. In a semiconductor heterostructure, band offsets can create that confinement. The following finite square well model makes the resulting discrete transverse energy levels explicit.

Thermal occupation of a quantum well (p1​/p0​=e−(E1​−E0​)/(kB​T))

Words: 59
Quantum well OurBigBook.com
For one nondegenerate thermalized particle, excited-state occupation relative to the ground state is set by the excitation gap, not by the absolute energy origin. In an infinite square well of width L, the first gap is 3π2ℏ2/(2mL2). Predominant ground-state occupation requires this gap to be much larger than kB​T; an explicit tolerated occupation gives a quantitative temperature criterion. State quantum degeneracy adds its statistical weight.

Quantum-confined Stark effect (ΔE=−p0​F−αX​F2/2+⋯)

Words: 66
Quantum well OurBigBook.com
An electric field normal to a semiconductor quantum well shifts the electron and hole confinement energies and displaces their envelopes in opposite directions. The exciton optical transition usually redshifts and its oscillator strength falls as their overlap decreases. In a symmetric unbiased well the permanent dipole p0​ vanishes, so the leading weak-field shift is quadratic. This optical shift includes confinement and binding changes; it is not solely a change in exciton binding energy.

Quantum-well interband threshold (Ej,nedge​)

Words: 30
Quantum well OurBigBook.com
For parabolic bands confined by an infinite well of width L, a same-index transition has edge Eg,j​+π2ℏ2n2(1/me∗​+1/mh,j∗​)/(2L2). Above it the in-plane pair kinetic energy is ℏ2k∥2​/(2μj​) with reduced mass μj−1​=(me∗​)−1+(mh,j∗​)−1.

Infinite-well interband selection rule

Words: 40
Quantum well OurBigBook.com
In an infinite square well, electron and hole envelopes are the same normalized sine functions even when their effective masses differ. In the electric dipole and envelope approximations, their overlap is ∫Fn′∗​(z)Fn​(z)dz=δn′n​. The same-index rule is an ideal-envelope rule, separate from Bloch-state polarization selection rules.

Envelope function approximation

Words: 43
Quantum well OurBigBook.com
A semiconductor state is approximated by a slowly varying envelope multiplying a cell-periodic Bloch function from a selected band. effective masses govern the envelope equation. Interband optical matrix elements then factor approximately into a cell-scale momentum matrix element and an envelope overlap; abrupt interfaces, band mixing and nonparabolicity limit the separation.

Finite-well confinement in a semiconductor heterostructure (z0​=a2m∗V0​​/ℏ)

Words: 322
Quantum well OurBigBook.com
Consider an original one-dimensional effective mass model with V(x)=0 for ∣x∣<a and V(x)=V0​>0 outside. Take the same positive effective mass m∗ everywhere, an abrupt interface, and no interactions. The wavefunction represents a transverse envelope; free motion parallel to the layer is outside this calculation. A double heterostructure laser need not be thin enough for this quantization to dominate its operation.
Set s=x/a, ϵ=ℏ2/(2m∗a2), z02​=V0​/ϵ, z2=E/ϵ and w=z02​−z2​. The time-independent Schrödinger equation becomes
−ds2d2ϕ​+u(s)ϕ=z2ϕ,u(s)={0z02​​∣s∣<1,∣s∣>1.​
(32)
Here u(s) denotes the dimensionless potential; a bound state has 0<z<z0​. Matching the wavefunction and its derivative at s=1 gives
ztanz=w(even),−zcotz=w(odd).
(33)
For the even bound state, the interior solution is Acos(zs) and the exterior solution is Acosze−w(∣s∣−1). For the odd bound state, replace cos(zs) by sin(zs) and cosz by sgn(s)sinz. The physical wavefunction is ψ(x)=ϕ(x/a)/a​.
Wavefunction normalization includes both exterior tails, not just the active layer. Direct integration gives
Aeven−2​=1+2zsin(2z)​+wcos2z​,Aodd−2​=1−2zsin(2z)​+wsin2z​.
(34)
The first two terms are the interior integral; the last is the total exterior integral. Thus the interior probability is Pin​=A2[1±sin(2z)/(2z)], with the upper sign for even parity.
Choose z0​=2. There is one even root in (0,π/2) and one odd root in (π/2,2); higher branches start beyond z0​. Each left-hand side increases on its stated interval while 4−z2​ decreases, proving uniqueness there. Numerically,
parityevenodd​z1.0298671.895494​E/V0​0.2651560.898225​Pin​0.9023170.451648​​
(35)
These are calculated values of the chosen finite square well. The excited bound state lies closer to the barrier and has a longer exterior tail: being bound does not mean having unit probability inside the well.
This model demonstrates electronic confinement, not optical refractive index confinement or a complete laser. Unequal effective masses, band bending, interface disorder and interactions require a more detailed model. In particular, continuity of the ordinary derivative above uses the chosen constant effective mass assumption.
